findings.title: Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Inside `concatenatedRSToASN1DER`, the two lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create throwaway ASN1Encoder instances, encode the BigIntegers into them, and then discard the result without ever using it - the method immediately re-creates new encoders a few lines below to build the actual return value. This is leftover/dead code that wastes CPU cycles on every signature conversion and signals the implementation wasn't cleaned up before merging; it should be removed.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: `CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` is documented (in the interface) as returning "BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider". This implementation instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a typical JVM resolves to the JDK's built-in keystore provider (e.g. SUN), not BouncyCastle at all. Unlike every other unimplemented method in this class, which consistently throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, this method silently returns a semantically wrong value, which can mislead any caller that relies on the contract (e.g. comparing/using the provider for BC-specific operations). It should either throw `UnsupportedOperationException` like the rest of the unimplemented methods, or be documented/implemented correctly.

findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks source compatibility for existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `CryptoProvider` is a public interface loaded via ServiceLoader/SPI and is implemented both inside and (potentially) outside this repository. Adding `int order();` as a new abstract method (no default implementation) means any existing implementation of this interface that is not updated in lock-step will fail to compile/break until it adds an `order()` override. Since this is a published API in the `common` module, this is a source-compatibility break for downstream custom CryptoProvider implementations. A default method (e.g. returning a baseline value) would avoid breaking existing implementors while still allowing providers that need preference to override it.

findings.title: Multiple CryptoProviders on classpath are now silently resolved instead of failing fast, with only debug-level logging
findings.body: Previously, `detectProvider` threw an `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found on the classpath, forcing an explicit fix of classpath/packaging issues. The new code silently picks the provider with the highest `order()` and only logs the ignored providers via `logger.debugf(...)`, which is typically disabled in production. This means a classpath misconfiguration that places two different CryptoProvider implementations on the classpath (e.g. accidentally bundling both FIPS and non-FIPS crypto modules) will no longer fail at startup and will instead silently run with whichever provider happens to have the higher `order()` value, without any visible warning in default logs. This can hide serious security/operational misconfigurations (e.g., running non-FIPS crypto when FIPS mode was intended) that used to be caught immediately.

findings.title: No test coverage for the new multi-provider ordering/selection logic
findings.body: `detectProvider` now sorts discovered `CryptoProvider` instances by `order()` (descending) and picks the first one instead of throwing when multiple are present. This is a meaningful behavioral change (see related finding about silent provider selection), but no unit test was added to verify that, given multiple CryptoProviders with different `order()` values on the classpath, the correct (highest-order) one is selected and the others are merely logged rather than causing failure.

findings.title: Single EC key pair of a default curve reused across ES256/ES384/ES512 tests
findings.body: The constructor generates a single `KeyPair` via `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` without specifying a curve, which will typically produce a P-256 (secp256r1) key pair. This same key pair is then reused for `testES256`, `testES384`, and `testES512`. Signing with SHA-384/SHA-512 using a P-256 key does not produce signatures whose R/S components match the natural lengths expected for ES384/ES512 (which are meant to be used with P-384/P-521 keys respectively). As a result, the tests don't exercise the ASN.1 encode/decode logic with realistically-sized R/S integers for the larger curves (e.g., the extra sign-byte handling that occurs with 66-byte P-521 integers), reducing the value of the ES384/ES512 test cases and potentially masking edge-case bugs that would only manifest with correctly-sized keys.
